chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Ibn Bukayr, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the lash (hudud) of a slave who threw accusations (at a free man). He said: 'He is lashed with eighty.' This is from the rights of people. As for what is from the rights of God, then he is lashed with half the punishment. I said: 'Which one is the one in which half the punishment is applied?' He said: 'When he commits zina (unlawful sexual intercourse) or drinks wine, this is from the rights of God in which half the punishment is applied.'

key_terms.حَدّ: Hudud: Fixed punishments for specific crimes
key_terms.حُرّ: Free man: A person who is not a slave
key_terms.حُقُوقِ اللَّهِ: Rights of God: Disputes or penalties arising from divine commandments
key_terms.حُقُوقِ النَّاسِ: Rights of people: Disputes or penalties arising from interpersonal rights
key_terms.زَنَى: Committed zina: Engaged in unlawful sexual intercourse
key_terms.قَذَفَ: Accused/Threw accusations: Specifically referring to qadhf (accusation of zina)
key_terms.مَمْلُوك: Slave: A male servant or bondman

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between hudud for rights of people and rights of God in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling to distinguish between hudud classified as 'rights of people' (huquq al-nas), such as false accusation (qadhf) by a slave against a free man, and 'rights of God' (huquq Allah), like zina or drinking wine. In the former, the slave receives the full 80 lashes, whereas in the latter, he receives half the standard penalty for a free person, reflecting the juristic principle that personal rights are not diminished by social status while divine rights are mitigated.
